A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ultrasound augmentation study and UltraBench benchmark. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and matchable, including retained Appendices A–D and v2's new Appendix E.

before.justification: v1 reports original augmentation experiments across seven classification and seven segmentation tasks, including individual augmentations and TrivialAugment, with 30 repetitions per condition.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds evaluations with larger EfficientNet and transformer models in Appendix E.

M1.justification: The augmentation procedures, ultrasound-specific transformations, and TrivialAugment procedure remain unchanged. Additional architectures are used to evaluate augmentation effectiveness, without introducing a new augmentation method.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 14 tasks from 10 datasets covering 11 body regions. Appendix E reuses classification and segmentation tasks from AUL Mass, CAMUS, and MMOTU. The revised description of convex and phased-array probes clarifies existing coverage.

E2.justification: The evaluated augmentation alternatives and no-augmentation controls remain the same, including single-augmentation and Top-N TrivialAugment comparisons. The added architectures change experimental configurations rather than the augmentation comparator set. Figure 9's added None markers redisplay controls already reported in Table 2.

E3.justification: Appendix E substantially extends evaluation beyond EfficientNet-B0 and its UNet counterpart to EfficientNet-B5, UNet with B5, MiT-B2, and SegFormer-B2. These additional experiments use 200 epochs and a seven-by-seven learning-rate and weight-decay grid search, distinct from the retained original Optuna protocol.

E4.justification: New Appendix E systematically examines sensitivity to model size and architecture on three differently sized datasets. Figures 13–16 test whether individual augmentation rankings and TrivialAugment's augmentation-set-size trends persist across models, extending v1's analyses of task and dataset dependence.

E5.justification: Tables 1, 2, 4, and 5 relabel their unchanged uncertainty values from standard deviation to standard error. v2 explicitly describes different random seeds for the existing 30 runs, adds baseline standard-error bands, and explains uncertainty-based effective/ineffective/harmful categories. An increased repetition count is not reported.

E6.justification: Tables 1, 2, 4, and 5 retain identical numerical entries, but Figures 13–16 add extensive results under new model and tuning settings. For example, AUL Mass classification ranks haze artifact highest with B5 and speckle reduction highest with MiT-B2. Figure 1 also changes brightness-adjustment usage from 9 to 11 studies and removes the separate two-study intensity-adjustment category.

T1.justification: The mathematical descriptions of the ultrasound augmentations, including Equations 1–5, are unchanged. No new theoretical assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs are introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's principal findings, and conclusion retain the same contributions: UltraBench, the effectiveness of conventional augmentations, task-dependent augmentation benefits, and useful gains from TrivialAugment. The new experiments support these claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: Appendix E newly interprets ranking differences through model-specific robustness and recommends architecture-specific augmentation selection. Section 7.2 adds computational-cost considerations with an explicit informal-benchmarking caveat. Section 7.3 drops the specific three-to-five-augmentation recommendation, and Section 7.1 clarifies that classification and segmentation use different performance metrics.

D1.justification: Table 3 adds Albumentations class mappings and explicit flip entries without changing augmentation parameters. v2 documents the added experiments' search settings and newly states minimum training duration and convergence for existing experiments. Section 7.2 reports an informal 1.5–2× speckle-reduction slowdown for smaller models. Code-access information remains available.

R1.justification: v2 adds Xie et al. (2021), the SegFormer reference supporting the new transformer evaluations. The substantive positioning against earlier augmentation studies remains stable; other bibliography edits largely concern metadata and formatting.

P1.justification: v2 condenses and rewrites parts of the background, edits dataset descriptions and recommendations, removes a repetitive results paragraph, and adds publication information and Appendix E. The main section sequence and overall narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds four substantial multipanel figures for architecture experiments. Existing result plots gain baseline uncertainty bands, explicit control markers, and colored shapes distinguishing augmentation categories. Table 3 gains an implementation column, while classification displays standardize their metric labels to mAP.

improvement.justification: Appendix E strengthens the evidence beyond v1's single small backbone, while consistent uncertainty descriptions, clearer plots, and implementation mappings improve interpretability and reproducibility. These are useful, targeted gains: architecture checks cover three retained datasets, timing evidence remains informal, and the central experimental results and conclusions remain stable.
